key_works: The California Critical Thinking Dispositions Inventory (1992)
The Disposition Toward Critical Thinking (1992, Journal of General Education)
distinctive_feature: The first rigorously validated instrument for measuring CT dispositions rather than CT skills — measuring the motivational/attitudinal preconditions for critical thinking, not the ability to think critically.
description: The CCTDI was developed directly from the Delphi Project's identification of critical thinking dispositions as a distinct and essential component of CT competence. Facione and Facione recognized that existing CT assessments (including the Watson-Glaser) measured skill and ability, but left untouched the question of whether individuals were disposed to apply those skills. A person can possess excellent CT skills and nonetheless be disinclined to seek truth, close-minded to alternative perspectives, or disorganized in their approach. The CCTDI measures these dispositional orientations through 75 self-report items across seven subscales.
dewey_connection: Dewey's conception of the reflective thinker was always holistic — the genuine inquirer was not merely skilled but was characterized by 'the desire to inquire,' 'intellectual honesty,' and 'persistence in doubt.' The CCTDI operationalizes these Deweyan character traits into measurable subscales.
core_finding: The CCTDI's most significant research finding is that disposition predicts whether skills are deployed better than skills predict whether they are deployed. A highly disposed but moderately skilled thinker will think critically more often than a highly skilled but poorly disposed thinker. Disposition is not a supplement to skill — it is a prerequisite for the consistent application of skill.

instrument_overview.format: Self-report Likert scale (6-point: Strongly Agree to Strongly Disagree)
instrument_overview.scoring: Subscale scores of 40+ indicate positive disposition; overall scores of 280+ indicate positive overall CT disposition
instrument_overview.scoring_note: Items are worded both positively and negatively with scoring direction adjusted accordingly

seven_subscales.name: Truth-Seeking
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to follow evidence wherever it leads, even when that destination is uncomfortable or contrary to one's current beliefs or self-interest.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Prioritizing what is true over what is convenient, comfortable, or self-affirming
behavioral_indicators: Actively seeks disconfirming evidence for one's own conclusions
Changes position when evidence warrants, regardless of social cost
Asks difficult questions even when the answers might be unwelcome
Acknowledges uncertainty and limits of one's own knowledge
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Confirmation bias, motivated reasoning, selective attention to supporting evidence, intellectual dishonesty
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder intellectual virtues: Intellectual Honesty, Intellectual Courage, Fair-mindedness

seven_subscales.name: Open-mindedness
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to seriously entertain and fairly evaluate perspectives, viewpoints, and arguments that differ from one's current position.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Genuine consideration of alternatives — not mere tolerance of them
behavioral_indicators: Gives serious consideration to views that conflict with personal beliefs
Tries to understand a position before critiquing it
Recognizes that one's own perspective may be limited or biased
Distinguishes between 'I disagree' and 'this is unreasonable'
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Dogmatism, strawmanning, premature dismissal of alternatives, intellectual arrogance
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Empathy, Fair-mindedness, Intellectual Humility

seven_subscales.name: Analyticity
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to apply reason and evidence in problem-solving, the alertness to problematic situations, and the anticipation of potential consequences.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: A standing inclination to approach situations with analytical reasoning rather than intuition or impulse
behavioral_indicators: Recognizes when careful analysis is needed, even in apparently simple situations
Anticipates potential problems and unintended consequences
Applies evidence and reasoning to novel problems
Resists the pull of simplistic or emotionally appealing solutions
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Impulsive decision-making, failure to anticipate consequences, over-reliance on intuition
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Diligence, Applying Intellectual Standards

seven_subscales.name: Systematicity
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to approach problem-solving and inquiry in an organized, focused, and diligent manner.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Orderly, disciplined engagement with complex problems rather than fragmented or disorganized thinking
behavioral_indicators: Organizes complex problems before attempting to solve them
Maintains focus on the central question throughout an inquiry
Follows through on reasoning chains rather than abandoning incomplete analysis
Uses structured approaches to evidence gathering and evaluation
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Scattered thinking, failure to follow through, confusion of central and peripheral issues, intellectual disorganization
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Diligence, Intellectual Perseverance

seven_subscales.name: CT Self-Confidence
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to trust in one's own reasoning processes — to believe that one's careful reasoning is generally reliable and that conclusions arrived at through good reasoning are worth standing behind.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Faith in the value of one's own careful thought — not arrogance, but confidence in process
behavioral_indicators: Willing to defend reasoned conclusions against social pressure
Does not abandon a position merely because others disagree
Trusts the results of one's own careful analysis
Distinguishes between genuine reconsideration and social capitulation
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Intellectual timidity, over-deferring to authority, abandoning well-reasoned positions under social pressure
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Autonomy, Intellectual Courage
seven_subscales.important_caveat: CT self-confidence must be calibrated to the actual quality of one's reasoning. Confidence in poor reasoning is intellectual arrogance, not CT self-confidence.

seven_subscales.name: Inquisitiveness
seven_subscales.description: Intellectual curiosity — the disposition to want to know more, to be interested in topics beyond their immediate utility, and to find intellectual investigation intrinsically rewarding.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Valuing learning and understanding for its own sake
behavioral_indicators: Pursues questions and topics even without immediate practical application
Reads and learns beyond assigned or required material
Asks 'why' and 'what if' even when the answer doesn't affect an immediate decision
Finds intellectual exploration enjoyable rather than effortful
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Intellectual incuriosity, learning only what is immediately required, treating knowledge as purely instrumental
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Perseverance, Intellectual Humility (recognizing what one does not know)

seven_subscales.name: Maturity of Judgment
seven_subscales.description: The disposition to apply careful judgment even in uncertain situations, to approach problems with appropriate caution and complexity, and to recognize that some questions do not have simple right/wrong answers.
seven_subscales.core_commitment: Epistemic sophistication — neither dogmatic certainty nor paralyzing relativism
behavioral_indicators: Tolerates ambiguity without demanding premature closure
Recognizes that prudent decisions can be made even under genuine uncertainty
Distinguishes between situations that require careful deliberation and those that don't
Accepts that reasonable people can disagree on some questions
seven_subscales.deficit_manifestation: Premature closure, black-and-white thinking, both dogmatism (false certainty) and paralysis (false relativism)
seven_subscales.paul_elder_connection: Maps to Paul-Elder: Intellectual Humility, Fairmindedness
seven_subscales.connection_to_developmental_models: High maturity of judgment corresponds to Perry's commitmentwithin-relativism stage — the capacity to act decisively while maintaining openness to revision

research_findings.finding: Disposition predicts skill deployment better than skill predicts deployment
research_findings.implication: CT education that targets only skills while neglecting dispositions is building an engine that may never be turned on

research_findings.finding: Overall CCTDI score is more strongly correlated with academic achievement than GPA in some studies
research_findings.implication: Dispositional orientation to inquiry may be a more fundamental predictor of intellectual performance than past performance

research_findings.finding: Truth-seeking is the subscale most strongly correlated with overall CT skill score
research_findings.implication: The motivation to follow evidence is both the most foundational disposition and the one most tightly linked to actual reasoning ability

research_findings.finding: CT self-confidence is the subscale most variable across professional populations
research_findings.implication: Context and culture significantly affect willingness to defend reasoned positions — intellectual environments matter

common_misconceptions.misconception: High CCTDI scores mean someone is a skilled critical thinker.
common_misconceptions.correction: The CCTDI measures only disposition — the motivational and attitudinal orientation toward CT. High disposition scores do not guarantee high CT skill scores. Both must be measured separately.
common_misconceptions.practical_implication: Assess both disposition (CCTDI) and skill (Watson-Glaser, Halpern) for a complete picture of CT capacity.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Dispositional development requires separate instruction from skill development.
common_misconceptions.correction: Dispositions develop through the same engagement that develops skills — but only if the engagement creates genuine intellectual challenge, requires truth-seeking in the face of uncertainty, and rewards intellectual honesty rather than performance.
common_misconceptions.practical_implication: Classroom culture, feedback practices, and task design all affect dispositional development. Skills instruction in a closed, right-answer culture can actually harm dispositions.

app_usage.primary_use: Self-assessment framework for identifying dispositional strengths and development areas
app_usage.exercise_integration: CCTDI subscales appear in self-reflection prompts and portfolio entries. The 'Intellectual Character' section of the app is organized around CCTDI subscales.
app_usage.cross_reference: Compare with Delphi Consensus Framework (source of CCTDI dispositions), Paul-Elder Intellectual Virtues (overlapping character traits), Habits of Mind (Costa & Kallick — related dispositional framework).
app_usage.self_assessment_prompt: Rate yourself on each subscale: which dispositions are your strongest? Which are you most likely to compromise under social pressure or when the inquiry is uncomfortable? Truth-seeking is typically the hardest — when did you last seriously seek out evidence that could prove you wrong?
